The first `console.log` runs while `isReady` is still `true`, so that's what it captures and prints — it doesn't somehow know the value will change two lines later. Then `isReady` is reassigned to `false`, and the second `console.log` runs after that reassignment, printing the new value. Each print statement only ever reports what's true at the exact moment it runs.

prompt: It's 11pm, you're on your phone at 20% battery, and you want to try one line of code before you're too foggy to keep going. Which setup actually gets you there tonight?

options.text: Download and install a code editor on your phone first
Open a browser-based editor and start typing — nothing to install
Wait until you're at a laptop with more battery and better focus
Set up a terminal on your phone first, since that's the "real" way to code

hints: A browser-based editor runs entirely on someone else's server — your phone just needs a browser and a connection.
What's the actual blocker in each option — time, battery, or something else? Which option removes the most blockers right now?
explanation: A browser-based editor. It runs in someone else's data center, not on your phone, so there's nothing to download and no install to wait through — you open a page and start typing. Waiting for "better conditions" is a reasonable instinct sometimes, but it also means tonight's ten minutes never happen, and a phone's browser is a completely real place to write and run a first program. Terminals matter later (lesson 3), but they're not the requirement to get started tonight.

prompt: True or false: a browser-based editor is just a toy version of "real" coding, meant for beginners only.

config.statement: Browser-based editors are a toy version of coding, not something used for real work.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and gives a concrete reason tied to what the code actually is (real, running code) rather than where it's typed.

hints: Does the code you write in a browser-based editor actually run — does it produce real output?
Plenty of working professionals build and share things using browser-based tools daily. What would make something "not real" coding?
explanation: False. The code itself doesn't know or care where it was typed — a program that adds two numbers does exactly the same thing whether it was written in a browser tab or an installed application. Browser-based editors are used by working developers for real projects, prototypes, and teaching, not only by beginners. The tempting belief here mistakes "more setup steps" for "more legitimate," when the setup steps are actually unrelated to whether the resulting code is real.

prompt: Put these steps for installing VS Code (a free code editor) in the order you'd actually do them.

items: Download the installer from the official VS Code website
Run the installer and follow its prompts
Open VS Code once it's installed
Create or choose a folder for your project
Open that folder inside VS Code

hints: You can't run an installer you haven't downloaded, and you can't open a folder in an editor that isn't open yet.
This is the same top-to-bottom idea from Module 1 — each step needs the one before it to have already happened.
explanation: Download, install, open, create or pick a folder, then open that folder inside the editor. Each step depends on the one before it existing: you can't run an installer that hasn't downloaded, and there's nothing to open a folder inside until the editor itself is open. This is the same top-to-bottom logic Module 1 covered for code — it applies just as much to the steps of setting a tool up.

prompt: A learner installs VS Code in the middle of a bad flare, gets stuck on a confusing installer screen, and concludes they're "just not cut out for this." What actually went wrong?

options.text: They genuinely lack the aptitude for coding
They tried a new, unfamiliar task during low capacity, which is hard regardless of skill
VS Code is too complicated for beginners and they should have used something else
Installing software always goes wrong the first time

hints: Would the exact same installer screen be confusing on a good day too, or mostly on a foggy one?
What does this say about the timing of the attempt, rather than about the learner or the tool?
explanation: They attempted an unfamiliar task — reading an installer, making choices, troubleshooting if something looks odd — during a stretch with the least capacity to handle exactly that kind of task. That's a timing mismatch, not a verdict on ability. New, fiddly tasks are disproportionately hard on a bad day for anyone, which is exactly why installing isn't something you're required to do today: it's fine to wait for a day with more room in it, and use the browser-based editor from lesson 1 in the meantime.

prompt: Match each terminal command to what it actually does.

pairs.right: Lists what's inside the current folder
Moves into a folder named project-name
Creates a new folder named project-name
Runs the JavaScript file app.js and shows its output

hints: pwd stands for "print working directory" — it's asking the terminal where it thinks you are.
cd stands for "change directory" — moving is different from listing, which is different from creating.
explanation: Five commands, five distinct jobs: pwd tells you where you are, ls shows what's around you there, cd moves you somewhere else, mkdir makes a new place to be, and node app.js runs an actual program. Nothing here overlaps — each one answers a different question ("where am I", "what's here", "go somewhere else", "make a new place", "run this file"), which is exactly why five commands cover a surprising amount of ground for a beginner.

prompt: You type `sd my-project` into the terminal, meaning to move into that folder, and it responds with something like "command not found: sd". What actually happened?

options.text: The terminal is broken and needs restarting
"my-project" doesn't exist as a folder
You typed "sd" instead of "cd" — the terminal only recognizes exact commands it knows
The command worked, but silently did nothing

hints: The terminal is telling you, plainly, that "sd" isn't a command it recognizes — read that message literally.
Compare the two letters at the start of "sd" against the command you meant to type.
explanation: "sd" isn't a real command — it's a one-letter typo of "cd". The terminal isn't being difficult or broken; it's telling you, accurately, that it has no command called "sd" in its vocabulary. This is worth getting used to early: the terminal only ever recognizes the exact words it knows, and a single wrong letter produces an error that looks alarming but means something very ordinary — "that's not a word I know." Module 4 goes deep on reading messages like this; for now, the fix is almost always: check the spelling.

prompt: You save a file called app.js from your editor. Later, in the terminal, you type `node app.js` and get "Cannot find module 'app.js'" — even though you can see the file open right in front of you in the editor. What's the most likely explanation?

options.text: The file is corrupted and needs to be rewritten
The terminal's current folder isn't the same folder the file was saved into
node.js doesn't actually work with files named app.js
The editor and the terminal are permanently unable to see the same files

hints: The terminal only looks inside the one folder it currently considers "here" — check that against where the file was actually saved.
This is exactly the situation pwd exists to check: where does the terminal think it is right now?
explanation: The terminal only looks for files inside whatever folder it currently considers "here" — and "here" for the terminal has nothing to do with which file happens to be open in your editor. If app.js was saved into a Downloads folder but the terminal is sitting in a different project folder, `node app.js` will fail even though the file genuinely exists somewhere. Running `pwd`, then `ls`, is the two-command habit that catches this instantly: it shows exactly where the terminal is and exactly what it can currently see.

prompt: Sort each filing habit by whether it tends to help future-you find things, or tends to create a mess that's hard to untangle later.

items.text: One project = one folder, everything for it lives inside
Descriptive, lowercase names with hyphens (grocery-list-app)
Saving new versions as final2, final2-ACTUAL, final2-use-this-one
Files scattered across Desktop, Downloads and Documents for the same project

hints: Ask: six months from now, with no memory of today, could you find the right file by its name and location alone?
"final2-ACTUAL-use-this-one" is a real thing people write, and it's a symptom, not a filing system.
explanation: One folder per project and clear, consistent names both answer the same question in advance: "where would future-you look?" Scattering files across default save locations, or renaming instead of genuinely versioning, both create the same failure later — multiple things that might be the real one, in different places, with no way to tell which is current without opening each one. A single project folder with sensible names is the whole fix, and it costs nothing extra to do from the start.

prompt: A default code editor loads with a bright white background, small text, and expects two hands for shortcuts. Which of these changes addresses an actual barrier, rather than being a cosmetic preference?

options.text: Switching to a dark theme when bright white screens are painful in low light or trigger light sensitivity
Switching fonts because the default one "looks unprofessional"
Making the window a different shade of blue for visual variety
Renaming the editor's icon

hints: Which of these changes affects whether the editor is actually usable for someone, versus how it looks to someone else?
Light sensitivity and eye strain are real, physical barriers to using a bright screen — not a matter of taste.
explanation: The dark theme change. Bright white interfaces cause real physical strain for a lot of people, and outright pain for anyone with light sensitivity — this isn't a style preference, it's the difference between a session that's usable and one that isn't. The other options are cosmetic: they might matter to someone's taste, but none of them change whether the editor can actually be used comfortably. Worth noticing the difference, because accessibility settings sometimes get dismissed as vanity when they're actually the thing making a session possible at all.

prompt: Describe your own realistic "bad day" coding setup in three sentences: what device, what theme/font settings, and what you'd do instead of typing if your hands aren't cooperating today (dictation, voice-to-text, autocomplete-heavy typing, or something else specific to you).
hints: Be concrete about the device — "my phone, propped on a pillow" is more useful to future-you than "something small."
If typing is hard some days, name the actual alternative you'd reach for, not just "I'd manage somehow."
This only has to work for you, on your worst realistic day — it doesn't need to look like anyone else's setup.
explanation: There's no single correct setup, but a genuinely useful answer is specific: names an actual device, states real settings (dark theme, a specific larger font size), and names a real fallback for hard-typing days rather than leaving that blank. What weakens an answer is vagueness — "whatever works" isn't something you can act on at 11pm with a foggy head. The whole point of writing this now is that a bad day doesn't have to include figuring this out from scratch.

prompt: You want to check which folder the terminal currently considers "here." Which command?

options.text: ls
pwd
cd
mkdir

hints: "Where am I" and "what's around me" are two different questions with two different commands.
explanation: pwd — it answers exactly "where is the terminal right now," which is the first thing to check whenever a file seems to have gone missing.

prompt: You want to see what files and folders exist inside the folder you're currently in. Which command?

options.text: pwd
ls
node
cd

hints: This is the "what's here" question, not the "where am I" or "go somewhere" question.
explanation: ls — it lists the contents of your current folder, which is how you confirm a file is actually where you expect before trying to run or open it.

prompt: Put these terminal actions in order to create a new project folder called my-app and move into it.
hints: You can't move into a folder that doesn't exist yet.
Checking where you ended up (pwd) is a reasonable last step, to confirm the move worked.
explanation: mkdir my-app first (create it), then cd my-app (move into it), then pwd as a sanity check that you actually landed where you meant to. Trying to cd into a folder before it exists just produces another "not found" style message.

prompt: True or false: if you can see a file open in your editor, the terminal will always be able to find and run it too.

config.statement: A file being open in your editor guarantees the terminal can find and run it.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains it in terms of the terminal's current folder, not just 'sometimes it doesn't work.'

hints: The editor opens a file directly by its full location. The terminal only sees what's inside whatever folder it currently considers "here."
Two separate tools, two separate ideas of "where things are" — being visible in one doesn't guarantee it's reachable from the other.
explanation: False. The editor can open a file from anywhere on the device directly. The terminal only ever looks inside its own current folder — if that folder isn't the one the file actually lives in, `node` will report it as missing even though it's genuinely there, just somewhere else. Checking with `pwd` and `ls` is how you confirm the two are actually looking at the same place.

prompt: Which filename would future-you (six months from now, no memory of today) most easily understand?

options.text: final2-ACTUAL-use-this.js
project1.js
grocery-list-total.js
asdf.js

hints: Which of these names describes what the file actually does, rather than just marking it as "a version" or being meaningless?
explanation: grocery-list-total.js — it describes what the file actually is, which is the entire test a good filename needs to pass. The others either describe a messy version history (final2-ACTUAL) or say nothing at all (project1, asdf).

prompt: Sort each setup choice by whether it addresses a real physical barrier or is purely cosmetic preference.

items.text: Switching to a dark theme for light sensitivity
Increasing font size because small text is hard to focus on for long
Picking a different accent color because you like it better
Relying more on autocomplete on a day typing is physically hard

hints: Ask of each: does this change whether the session is usable, or just how it looks?
explanation: Theme, font size for focus, and reduced reliance on precise typing all change whether a session is genuinely usable for a given body on a given day — that's the accessibility category. An accent color is a preference with no bearing on usability either way, which is the entire distinction worth holding onto.

prompt: In one sentence, what's the very first thing to check when the terminal says it can't find a file you know exists?
hints: Think back to the two-command habit from lesson 4.
explanation: Whether the terminal's current folder (checked with `pwd`) actually matches the folder the file is really saved in — the file usually exists, it's just not where the terminal is currently standing.

options.text: Only the first line, "Hello";
Only the second line, // Hello
Only the third line, console.log("Hello");
All three — they all mention the word Hello

hints: A `//` at the start of a line is a comment — the computer skips it entirely, it isn't executed at all.
A bare piece of text on its own line is technically valid, but nothing tells the computer to display it anywhere.
explanation: Only `console.log("Hello")`. The first line is valid but does nothing visible — nothing in it says "show this on screen," it just exists and is discarded. The second line is a comment (anything after `//`) and the computer skips it completely, as if it weren't there. `console.log(...)` is specifically the instruction "display this" — without it, a program can run correctly and produce absolutely nothing you can see.

prompt: Write the console.log line that would print exactly: Age: 34 (using a variable called age that already holds the number 34, combined with the label "Age: ").
hints: console.log can take more than one comma-separated value and will print them with a space between.
You don't need the + operator here at all if you use commas.
explanation: `console.log("Age:", age);` — passing "Age:" and `age` as two separate comma-separated values tells console.log to print both, with a space automatically inserted between them, producing "Age: 34". A common near-miss is writing `console.log("Age: " + age)`, which also works and prints the same thing — worth recognizing both are valid, they just combine the pieces differently (one string built with +, versus two separate values handed to console.log).

prompt: You have a working program: `let price = 10; console.log("Price:", price);` printing "Price: 10". Before touching anything, you're asked to predict: if you change `let price = 10;` to `let price = 10 + 5;`, what will print?

options.text: Price: 10
Price: 15
Price: 10 + 5
An error

hints: `10 + 5` is ordinary arithmetic here, with no quotes around either number — nothing stops it from being calculated.
The variable price ends up holding whatever the calculation produces, not the text of the calculation itself.
explanation: Price: 15. `10 + 5` is plain arithmetic — no quotes, no strings involved — so it's calculated to 15 before ever being stored in `price`. By the time console.log runs, `price` simply holds the number 15; it has no memory of having been written as "10 + 5". Predicting this before running it is exactly the habit this lesson is about: naming what you expect, so a surprising result tells you something real, rather than being the first time you've thought about it at all.

prompt: Put these steps in the order that keeps you from losing track of what actually caused a result, when changing a working program.

items: Confirm the current program works and note what it currently outputs
Run it and compare the new output to your prediction
If it matches, move on; if not, that one change is the only possible cause

hints: Notice how each step depends on there being exactly one variable that changed — what would break if you made three changes at once instead of one?
The whole value of this order is that a surprise can only point at one thing.
explanation: Confirm the starting point, change one thing, run and compare, then use the result. The entire value of this sequence is that a surprising result can only have one possible cause — the single thing you just changed. Change three things at once and a surprise leaves you with three suspects instead of one, which is exactly the situation the next pod covers.

options.text: It's factually wrong — the code doesn't add 1 to age
It just restates what the line already says, in plainer words, adding no new information
Comments aren't allowed directly above a line of code
It should be written in all capital letters to stand out

hints: Read the code line, then read the comment. Does the comment tell you anything the code didn't already say on its own?
A comment earns its place by adding something the code alone doesn't show — not by translating code into English.
explanation: It just restates the line in plainer words. `age = age + 1;` already says, unambiguously, "add 1 to age" — anyone who can read the code doesn't need the comment, and anyone who can't read the code won't understand the comment's reason for existing either. A comment worth writing answers a question the code itself can't: *why* is this happening here, what would break if it were removed, what edge case does this handle. "What this line does" is the code's job. "Why this line exists" is the comment's job.

prompt: Sort each comment by whether it's genuinely useful to future-you, or adds nothing beyond what the code already says.

items.text: // increment the counter by one   (above: counter = counter + 1;)
// using + 1 here, not + 1000ms, because the API returns whole seconds not milliseconds
// this looks redundant but the API sometimes returns the date twice — don't remove
// set name variable   (above: let name = "Alex";)

hints: Cover up the code and read only the comment — does it teach you something you couldn't already see from the line itself?
The useful ones explain a reason, a gotcha, or a non-obvious constraint. The useless ones just translate code into English.
explanation: The useful comments explain something invisible in the code alone: a unit mismatch that would be easy to get wrong, or a reason something that looks safe to delete actually isn't. The useless ones simply restate what the line already says in English, which anyone reading the code already knows. The test is always the same: would removing the comment lose real information, or just remove a redundant caption?

prompt: A working program has this line: `console.log("Total:", total);` You delete the closing parenthesis on purpose, on a throwaway copy, just to see what happens. What's the actual value of doing this?

options.text: None — deliberately breaking working code has no upside
It shows you what a specific kind of mistake looks like, on your own terms, before it happens by accident
It teaches the computer to recognize your personal coding style
It's only useful once you already know what every error means

hints: Think about the difference between meeting an error for the first time by accident under pressure, versus meeting the same error on purpose with nothing at stake.
What does this deliberate version give you that an accidental break later wouldn't?
explanation: It shows you what a specific mistake looks like on your own terms — calm, expected, nothing at stake — instead of meeting the exact same error for the first time by accident, mid-task, under pressure. You end up with a little library of "oh, I recognize this shape of problem" before Module 4 even formally covers error messages, which makes the real thing far less alarming when it happens later on something that actually matters to you.

prompt: True or false: once you've broken a program on purpose to experiment, it's fine to keep going without keeping a working copy anywhere.

config.statement: Once you're experimenting by breaking code on purpose, you don't need to keep an untouched working copy anywhere.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains what's lost if the only copy left is the broken one.

hints: If the experiment goes further than planned and you can't remember the working version, what's your way back?
This is the safety net that makes breaking things on purpose low-stakes in the first place.
explanation: False. The entire reason deliberate breaking is low-stakes is that a working version still exists somewhere to return to — a saved copy, or code you remember well enough to retype. Without that, an experiment that goes further than intended leaves you stuck with no way back, which turns a safe, curious exercise into an accidental, stressful one. Keeping an untouched copy costs seconds and is what makes "break it on purpose" worth doing at all.

prompt: You type `cons` and your editor offers to complete it to `console.log()` with the cursor already placed between the parentheses. For someone with limited hand stamina on a given day, what's the actual benefit here?

options.text: It teaches the computer your personal style over time
It reduces the physical typing required for something you'll type constantly, without changing what the code does
It makes the code run faster once the program starts
It's mainly a convenience for experienced programmers, not beginners

hints: Does accepting the suggestion change anything about what the finished code does, or only how much typing it took to get there?
console.log is something you'll type dozens of times a session — what does saving keystrokes on it actually cost, and what does it save?
explanation: It reduces physical typing for something you'll type over and over, with zero change to what the resulting code does — `console.log()` typed in full and `console.log()` completed from `cons` + tab are identical once they're on the page. For anyone whose hands don't always cooperate, or who's simply conserving effort for a session, that's a real, concrete accessibility win, not a lesser or lazier way to code. It's genuinely useful at every skill level, beginners included — arguably beginners most of all, since typing exact syntax correctly is still unfamiliar.

prompt: You paste a chunk of code from a tutorial into your project without reading it first, run it, and something unexpected happens — a variable you didn't expect got overwritten. What's the one habit that would have caught this before running it, and why does it matter more with pasted code than with code you typed yourself?
hints: Typing something yourself, even slowly, forces you to look at every line at least once. Pasting skips that entirely.
The habit isn't about distrust of the source — it's about knowing what's actually about to run in your own project.
explanation: The habit is reading pasted code before running it, the same way you'd read a paragraph before signing your name under it. It matters more with pasted code specifically because typing something yourself, even copying it slowly by hand, forces your eyes across every line at least once — pasting skips that step entirely, so code can land in your project and run without you having actually looked at it. This isn't about distrusting tutorials or AI-generated code (Module 5 covers working with AI help directly) — it's about knowing what's genuinely about to execute in your own project before it does, since you're the one who has to make sense of the result either way.

prompt: `let x = 5; console.log(x);` currently prints 5. Which single change makes it print 8?

options.text: Change console.log(x) to console.log(8)
Change let x = 5 to let x = 8
Add a comment saying // should be 8
Change console.log to console.print

hints: The most direct fix changes the actual stored value, not the printed label around it.
console.print isn't a real function — that option would break the program, not fix it.
explanation: Changing `let x = 5` to `let x = 8` — the cleanest fix changes the actual value stored in `x`, so anything using `x` downstream (including the console.log) reflects it correctly. Hardcoding `console.log(8)` would technically also print 8, but it disconnects the output from the variable entirely, which defeats the point of having a variable at all.

prompt: `let total = 4 + 4; console.log("Total:", total);` prints "Total: 8". Which single change makes it print "Total: 12" without changing the label?

options.text: Change "Total:" to "Total: 12"
Change 4 + 4 to 4 + 8
Change console.log to console.log12
Add a second console.log line with 12 in it

hints: The label "Total:" should stay exactly as it is — only the calculated value needs to change.
Whatever total ends up equaling is what gets printed next to the label.
explanation: Changing `4 + 4` to `4 + 8` (or any combination totaling 12) — this keeps the label intact and changes only the calculation feeding into `total`, so the output becomes "Total: 12" with nothing else disturbed. Rewriting the label itself would technically produce matching text but for the wrong reason — it stops being connected to an actual calculation at all.

prompt: `console.log("5" + 5);` currently prints "55". True or false: changing it to `console.log(5 + 5);` (removing the quotes) makes it print 10.

config.statement: Removing the quotes from console.log("5" + 5) so it reads console.log(5 + 5) makes it print 10.
config.rubric: A full answer confirms true and explains it via both values now being numbers rather than one being text.

hints: With the quotes removed, is either side of the + still text, or are both sides now plain numbers?
This is the same string-versus-number distinction from the Module 1 practice set, in reverse.
explanation: True. With the quotes removed, both 5s are plain numbers, so `+` performs ordinary addition instead of gluing text together — the result is 10. This is the exact inverse of the classic "5" + 3 surprise from earlier: quotes turn a value into text and change what `+` does to it; removing them restores ordinary arithmetic.

prompt: `let name = "Sam"; console.log("Hi " + name);` prints "Hi Sam". Which single change makes it print exactly "Hi Sam!" (with an exclamation mark, no extra space before it)?

options.text: Change "Hi " + name to "Hi " + name + "!"
Change let name = "Sam" to let name = "Sam!"
Add a new line: console.log("!");
Change "Hi " to "Hi !"

hints: The exclamation mark belongs at the very end of the greeting, joined onto what's already there.
Changing name itself would work for this one output, but it would put "!" inside the stored name, which is the wrong place for it.
explanation: Adding `+ "!"` onto the end of the existing line — this appends the exclamation mark exactly where it belongs, after the name, with no change to the name variable itself. Baking "!" into `name` would technically produce the right output here, but it corrupts what `name` actually represents (a name shouldn't include punctuation), which would cause problems anywhere else `name` gets used.

prompt: You're about to deliberately break a working program to see what a specific error looks like. Put these steps in the safe order.

items: Save or note the current working version
Run it and read what happens
Note what you changed and what resulted
Restore the working version before continuing

hints: The working version has to exist before you break anything, and it needs to come back after you're done looking.
This is lesson 4's safety habit, laid out as a literal sequence.
explanation: Save the working version first, break exactly one thing, observe the result, note what happened, then restore the working version before moving on. Skipping the first or last step is what turns a safe, deliberate experiment into an accidental, permanent mess.

prompt: Which comment is genuinely useful, not just a restatement of the code below it?

options.text: // create the name variable   (above: let name = "Sam";)
// keep this delay — the API needs a moment before the next call or it fails silently   (above: a short pause in the code)
// print the total   (above: console.log("Total:", total);)
// set price to 10   (above: let price = 10;)

hints: Cover the code and read only the comment — does it teach you something the code alone doesn't show?
explanation: The delay comment — it explains a non-obvious reason something exists ("the API needs a moment or it fails silently"), which is invisible from the code alone and would save real confusion if someone were tempted to remove it as pointless. The other three just translate their line into English, adding nothing a reader couldn't already see.

prompt: You're handed a chunk of code copied from a tutorial to paste into your project. Name the one thing you do before running it, and why that specific step matters more here than for code you type yourself.
hints: This is the same rule from lesson 5's second pod.
explanation: Read it, fully, before running it — because typing code yourself (even copying it slowly by hand) forces your eyes across every line at least once, and pasting skips that entirely. The step matters more for pasted code specifically because nothing else forces the look.

prompt: You want to type `console.log()` faster on a day your hands are tired. What's the actual mechanism that helps, without changing what the code does?

options.text: Autocomplete/snippets, which insert the full text from a short trigger
Writing shorter variable names throughout the program
Removing console.log calls you don't strictly need
Switching to a different programming language

hints: Which option reduces the physical typing for this exact instruction, without changing anything else about the program?
explanation: Autocomplete and snippets — typing a short trigger like `cons` and accepting the suggestion produces the identical `console.log()` with far less physical typing, and changes nothing about what the code does. Shorter variable names or removing console.log calls both change the actual program, which isn't what the situation calls for here.

prompt:
```
ReferenceError: total is not defined
    at Object.<anonymous> (/home/you/app.js:3:13)
```

Which part tells you exactly which file and line to go look at?

options.text: ReferenceError
total is not defined
/home/you/app.js:3:13
Object.<anonymous>

hints: The error type and the description both explain what went wrong. Only one part tells you where.
Look for a colon-separated pattern that ends in numbers — that's file, then line, then column.
explanation: The file path and numbers at the end: /home/you/app.js:3:13. This is the location — which file, which line (3), and even which character position on that line (13). "ReferenceError" names the category of problem, and "total is not defined" describes it in plain terms — both genuinely useful, but neither tells you where to go. The location is what turns a message into an actual next step: open that file, go to that line.

prompt: True or false: an error message like "ReferenceError: total is not defined" is the computer telling you that you made a mistake as a person.

config.statement: An error message is a judgment about you as a programmer, not just a description of what went wrong.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and connects it to the idea that error messages are generated, neutral text, not commentary.

hints: Where does the wording of an error message actually come from — is it written fresh each time about you specifically, or generated the same way for anyone who triggers that condition?
Would this exact same message appear for a senior developer who made the identical typo?
explanation: False. The exact same message — "ReferenceError: total is not defined" — would appear for absolutely anyone who triggered that condition, from someone on their first day to someone with twenty years of experience. It's generated text describing a specific, mechanical condition (a name was used that doesn't exist yet), with zero awareness of who wrote the code or why. Reading alarming tone into it is understandable — the wording can sound blunt — but there's no judgment encoded in it, only information.

prompt: A program has three console.log lines. Line 2 is missing a closing parenthesis. You run the whole file, and nothing prints at all — not even line 1's output, which had no problem of its own. Why not?

options.text: Line 1 also has a hidden mistake
The entire file has to be readable (parsed) before any of it can run — a syntax error blocks the whole file, not just the broken line
console.log only works if every line in the file is a console.log
Line 1's output printed but scrolled off screen

hints: Think back to Module 1: does the engine run line by line as it reads, or does something have to happen to the whole file first?
A syntax error means the engine can't even understand the shape of the code — not that it ran and then hit trouble.
explanation: The entire file has to successfully parse — be recognized as valid, readable code — before any of it runs. A syntax error means the engine can't make sense of the file's structure at all, so it never gets to "running" in the first place. This is different from Module 1's top-to-bottom execution model, which only applies once a program actually starts running. A syntax error happens one step earlier, before execution begins, which is exactly why a broken line 2 can silence a perfectly fine line 1.

options.text: message is spelled wrong
The opening quote before "Hello" is never matched by a closing quote — it swallows the rest of the line
console.log can't print a message with a comma in it
Two variables can't share a similar name

hints: Count the quotation marks in the first line carefully — there should be two, one to open the string and one to close it.
The exclamation mark at the end has a stray quote character right after "welcome" that never gets closed.
explanation: There's only one quote mark before "Hello," and none after "welcome!" to close it — the string never ends, so everything after it, including the semicolon and the rest of the file, gets swallowed into an unterminated piece of text, which the engine can't parse. This is one of the most common syntax slips: an opening quote with no matching close. Most editors highlight matched quotes and brackets in a different color specifically to catch this before you even run the file — worth actually looking at that highlighting rather than typing past it.

prompt: A program has four console.log lines. Lines 1 and 2 print successfully. Then a TypeError appears, and lines 3 and 4 never print. What kind of error is this most likely to be, and how do you know?

options.text: A syntax error — the file couldn't be read
A runtime error — the file parsed fine and started executing, then broke partway through
Not a real error — some lines printed, so the program basically worked
Impossible to tell without more information

hints: A syntax error blocks the entire file from running at all. Did that happen here?
Two lines genuinely printed before anything went wrong — what does that tell you about whether the file was readable in the first place?
explanation: A runtime error. The fact that lines 1 and 2 actually printed proves the file was successfully parsed and execution genuinely began — a syntax error would have blocked all four lines, including the first two. Something specific, encountered partway through running the program (not while reading it), caused the failure. "How far did it get before it broke" is one of the single most useful diagnostic questions you can ask of any error.

prompt: Match each runtime error message to the situation most likely to cause it.

pairs.right: Using a variable that was never created (or was misspelled) anywhere in the file

pairs.left: TypeError: greet is not a function
pairs.right: Trying to call something as a function that isn't one — often a typo, or the value is something else entirely

pairs.left: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')
pairs.right: Trying to access a property on a value that turned out to be undefined

hints: ReferenceError is about a name the engine has never seen before. TypeError is about doing something to a value that its actual type can't support.
"Cannot read properties of undefined" always means: something you expected to hold a real object turned out to hold nothing.
explanation: Each error type points at a different category of mistake. ReferenceError means the name itself was never established — a genuine typo or a variable used before it existed. TypeError covers a broad family of "you tried to do something this value's actual type doesn't support" — calling a non-function as if it were one, or reaching for a property on something that's currently undefined. Recognizing the error type narrows down what kind of mistake to look for before you've even read the specific variable names involved.

prompt: A stack trace lists several "at ..." lines: some mention internal library code, and one near the bottom mentions your own file, app.js. As a beginner just starting to read stack traces, which line is the most useful place to start looking?

options.text: The very first "at" line, regardless of which file it mentions
The line that mentions your own file — app.js — since that's the code you actually wrote and can change
Whichever line has the longest file path
None of them — stack traces with multiple lines can't be read by beginners

hints: You can't edit library or internal code — only your own file. Which line points at something you're actually able to act on?
A stack trace often includes frames from code you didn't write at all. Which one is worth your attention first?
explanation: The line mentioning your own file. A stack trace can include several frames from library or internal code you didn't write and generally can't (or shouldn't) edit — those explain the chain of calls, but they're not actionable for you directly. The frame naming your own file is the one place you can actually make a change, which makes it the practical place to start, even if it's not literally the first line printed.

prompt: A program has a function `getGreeting` that calls `formatName`, which calls `capitalize`, where the error actually happens. Reading the stack trace from the entry point outward, put these calls in the order they happened — from your original call down to where the failure occurred.

items: capitalize() — where the error actually occurred

hints: Start from the outermost call — the one closest to your own top-level code — and work inward toward where things actually broke.
Each function in this chain called the next one, one level deeper, until the error occurred at the innermost point.
explanation: Your top-level code called getGreeting(), which called formatName(), which called capitalize(), where the error actually occurred. A stack trace exists to show this exact chain: reading from your own entry point (often nearer the bottom of the printed trace) toward the specific inner call where things broke (nearer the top) tells the whole story of how the program arrived at the failure, one call at a time.

prompt:
Which search query is most likely to find genuinely useful results for this error?

`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toUpperCase') at /home/roi/my-grocery-app/index.js:14:23`

options.text: The entire error message pasted exactly, including the file path and line numbers
"TypeError Cannot read properties of undefined toUpperCase"
"my code is broken help"
"my-grocery-app error"

hints: Your file path and project name are unique to you — nobody else's search results will match them.
Keep the parts of the message that would be identical for anyone hitting the same underlying problem.
explanation: The error type plus the general description, with the personal specifics stripped out. Your file path (/home/roi/my-grocery-app/index.js) and exact line number are unique to your project and won't match anything anyone else has written about. The parts worth keeping are the parts that would be identical for anyone hitting this exact class of problem: the error type and the general phrase describing it. Vague queries like "my code is broken" have nothing specific enough to search against at all.

prompt: True or false: if a search result's code looks similar to yours and is confidently written, it's safe to assume it's a correct fix without checking anything else.

config.statement: A confidently written search result with similar-looking code is safe to trust without further checking.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and names at least one thing worth checking beyond how confident or similar the result looks.

hints: Confidence in how something is written says nothing about whether it's actually correct, or even about the same language or version.
What would you want to check about a result before trusting it — age, source, whether it matches your exact error?
explanation: False. How confident a result sounds has no bearing on whether it's actually correct — and "looks similar" can hide real differences: a different language, an outdated version, or a fix for a superficially similar but genuinely different error. Worth checking before trusting a result: does it mention your exact error type and message, is it reasonably recent, and does it come from a source with some accountability (official docs, a well-established Q&A site) rather than an anonymous, unverified post. None of that takes long, and skipping it is how a wrong fix gets pasted in and read before it runs — which is exactly the discipline Module 3 already covered for any pasted code.

prompt:
```
console.log("Total: " + total)
```
Running this produces: `ReferenceError: total is not defined`. What's the fix?

options.text: Remove console.log entirely
Add a line before it that creates total, e.g. let total = 10 + 5;
Change total to Total (capitalized)
Add quotes around total

hints: ReferenceError specifically means the name was never created anywhere the engine has seen yet.
Capitalizing it doesn't create it — it would just be a different, equally undefined name.
explanation: Add a line before it that actually creates `total` with a value. ReferenceError means the engine genuinely has no record of that name existing — not a spelling mismatch, an actual absence. Capitalizing it would just rename the problem to `Total is not defined`. Quoting it would turn it into the literal text "total" rather than the calculated value you actually want.

options.text: Add the missing closing parenthesis: console.log("Hi " + name);
Change name to Name
Delete the console.log line entirely
Add a semicolon after Sam

hints: Count the opening and closing parentheses on the console.log line — are they matched?
Nothing printing at all, including line 1's assignment, points at a syntax error, not a naming problem.
explanation: Add the missing closing parenthesis. The console.log call opens with `(` and never closes it, which is a syntax error — the file can't be parsed at all, which is exactly why nothing prints, not even something unrelated like `let name = "Sam"`. This matches lesson 2's core lesson: a syntax error blocks the entire file.

options.text: greet needs to be spelled differently
greet holds a piece of text, not a function — calling it with () doesn't make sense for that type of value
The semicolon is in the wrong place
console.log is missing

hints: What kind of value does greet actually hold right now — and does that kind of value support being "called" with parentheses?
TypeError means the value's actual type can't support what you're trying to do with it.
explanation: `greet` holds a string, "Hello" — and strings aren't functions, so `greet()` (attempting to call it as one) doesn't make sense for that type of value, exactly what TypeError signals. This is a common name collision: if `greet` were meant to be a function (`function greet() { ... }`), this variable — also named `greet` — would need a different name, or the function definition would need to come first and not be overwritten.

options.text: toString isn't a real function
user.age was never set, so it's undefined — and undefined has no toString to call
user.name should have been used instead, purely by coincidence
The object needs curly braces around age

hints: user only has a name property defined — what does user.age evaluate to if it was never set?
"Cannot read properties of undefined" always means something you expected to hold a real value turned out to hold nothing.
explanation: `user` only has a `name` property — `age` was never set on it, so `user.age` evaluates to `undefined`. Trying to call `.toString()` on `undefined` fails, because `undefined` doesn't have that method (or any methods) to call. The fix is either adding an `age` property to `user`, or checking that `user.age` actually holds something before calling a method on it.

prompt: A program has five console.log lines. The first three print, then a TypeError appears and lines 4 and 5 never run. True or false: this is a syntax error.

config.statement: A program where the first three of five console.log lines print before an error appears is a syntax error.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains using the syntax-vs-runtime distinction from lesson 2 and 3.

hints: A syntax error would have blocked the entire file, including the lines that printed fine.
Something printing at all is proof the file was successfully parsed and execution genuinely began.
explanation: False — this is a runtime error. A syntax error blocks the entire file before any of it runs, which would mean none of the five lines printed, not even the first three. The fact that three lines genuinely printed proves the file parsed successfully and execution began; something specific went wrong partway through running it, which is exactly what a runtime error is.

prompt: A stack trace has four "at" lines: three mention internal Node.js modules, and one — the third from the top — mentions your file, script.js, at line 9. Where should you look first?

options.text: The very first line of the trace, regardless of which file it names
The line naming script.js at line 9 — the code you actually wrote and can change
The very last line of the trace
None of them — start over from scratch instead

hints: Which of the four lines points at code you're actually able to edit?
explanation: The line naming script.js — it's the only frame in this trace pointing at code you actually wrote and can change. The internal module frames provide context about the call chain but aren't something you can act on directly.

prompt: Write a search query for this error, keeping only the parts that would help anyone with the same underlying problem: `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'price') at /Users/jo/shop-app/cart.js:22:10`
hints: Strip the file path, the project name, and the line number — none of those are shared with anyone else's project.
Keep the error type and the general shape of the description.
explanation: Something close to: TypeError Cannot read properties of undefined reading price — or even more generally, TypeError Cannot read properties of undefined. The file path (/Users/jo/shop-app/cart.js), the line number, and the specific property name are all details unique to this project; keeping the error type and general phrasing is what makes the search actually match what other people have written about the same class of problem.

prompt: You find a five-year-old forum post with a confident-sounding fix for your exact error message. What's the most reasonable next step?

options.text: Paste it in immediately — it matches your error exactly, and it sounds sure of itself
Check whether it's still relevant to your current setup, then read it carefully before running it
Ignore it entirely just because of its age, regardless of content
Post your entire project asking someone else to fix it for you

hints: Age alone doesn't disqualify a fix, but it's a reason to check rather than assume — same for how confident it sounds.
Whatever you do decide to use still needs the read-before-you-run rule from Module 3.
explanation: Check its relevance, then read it before running it. Age is a reason to verify, not an automatic disqualifier — some fixes remain valid for years, others don't. Confidence in tone tells you nothing reliable either way. Whatever you ultimately decide is worth trying still goes through the same rule Module 3 established for any pasted code: read it before it runs, regardless of how sure the source sounded.

prompt:
Two ways to ask an AI tool for help with a broken program:

**A:** "My code doesn't work, please fix it."

**B:** "This program should print a total but instead I get `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'price')` — here's the code: [pasted code]. I expected it to print the total price."

Which is more likely to get an answer that actually addresses your specific problem?

options.text: A — it's shorter, so the AI can focus on the core issue faster
B — it includes the actual code, the actual error, and what was expected
Both are equally likely to work — AI tools can infer the rest either way
Neither — AI tools need the entire project's history to help with anything

hints: Think back to Module 1: what does an instruction need in order for something with zero ability to guess to act on it correctly?
"Doesn't work" could mean dozens of different things. Which prompt actually narrows that down?
explanation: Prompt B. This mirrors exactly what Module 1 established about instructions in general: a request with no gaps left for guessing gets a useful response; a vague one forces whatever's on the other end to guess, and an AI tool guessing produces generic, often unhelpful advice — the equivalent of "have you tried turning it off and on again." Prompt B includes the actual code, the actual error message (Module 4's skill of reading it precisely pays off directly here), and what you expected instead — three concrete anchors a vague request simply doesn't have.

prompt: You're stuck on a program that should greet a user by name but instead prints "Hi undefined". Write the actual request you'd send an AI tool — include what you'd paste and what you'd say about what you expected.
hints: Include the actual code, not a description of it — "a variable that holds a name" is much less useful than the real line.
State clearly what you expected to see versus what you actually got — "Hi Priya" versus "Hi undefined".
If you have an error message (even if this case doesn't produce one), that goes in too.
explanation: A strong request pastes the actual code (not a paraphrase), states plainly what happened ("Hi undefined" printed) versus what was expected ("Hi Priya"), and — if there's an error message — includes that verbatim too. What weakens a request: describing the code in words instead of pasting it, or skipping the "expected vs actual" comparison entirely and just saying "it's wrong." The AI can only work with what's actually in front of it, and "undefined" appearing where a name should be is a genuinely useful, specific clue once it's stated plainly.

prompt: You paste an AI's fix into your program, it works, and you move on. A week later the exact same bug shows up in a different program, and you have no idea how to fix it. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: AI-generated fixes only work once and stop working afterward
The fix was applied without ever asking why it worked, so nothing about the underlying pattern was learned
The two bugs must be genuinely unrelated, despite looking identical
Programming knowledge naturally fades within a week regardless of how it was learned

hints: A fix and an explanation are two different things you can ask for. Which one did the first request actually get?
Copying a working line changes your file. It doesn't automatically change what you understand.
explanation: The fix worked and got applied, but nothing was ever asked about *why* it worked — so the underlying pattern never made it from "a line I pasted" into "something I understand." This is the practical difference between requesting a fix and requesting an explanation: a fix changes your file; an explanation changes what you can do next time, on your own, without pasting anything.

prompt: Sort each request by whether it's likely to get you a fix only, or a fix plus real understanding.

items.text: "Fix this."
"Here's my broken code and the error — please just give me working code."
"Here's my broken code and the error — explain why it's happening before giving me the fix."
"Fix this, and tell me what pattern I should watch for so I catch it myself next time."

hints: A request that only asks for corrected code, even a detailed one, is still only asking for a fix.
The requests that add understanding explicitly ask for the why, not just the what.
explanation: The difference isn't length or politeness — it's whether the request explicitly asks for the reasoning behind the fix, not just the corrected code itself. A detailed bug report that still only asks "give me working code" will usually get exactly that: working code, with no explanation attached unless it's specifically requested.

prompt: An AI gives you a five-line fix using a technique you've never seen before. You don't fully understand every detail of it yet. Which of these can you still reasonably check, without understanding every line?

options.text: Nothing — if you don't fully understand it, you can't check anything about it
Whether it actually runs without an error, and whether the output matches what you expected
Whether the AI "seemed confident" while explaining it
Whether it's the shortest possible way to solve the problem

hints: Running the code and comparing its output to what you expected doesn't require understanding every syntax detail first.
Confidence in tone is not something you can verify — it's not a property of the code at all.
explanation: Whether it runs and whether the output matches what you expected — both are checkable without full understanding of every line, using nothing more than the skills already built in this course: run it (Module 1), read any error carefully if one appears (Module 4), and compare the actual result to what you expected (Module 3's predict-first habit). Full line-by-line understanding is worth building toward, but it's not a prerequisite for a first, genuinely useful check.

prompt: True or false: if you don't fully understand a piece of AI-generated code yet, the safest thing is to avoid using it at all.

config.statement: Not fully understanding a piece of AI-generated code means you shouldn't use it at all.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and names at least one real check that doesn't require full understanding, rather than treating full understanding as all-or-nothing.

hints: Is there a meaningful middle ground between "understand every detail" and "blindly trust it"?
What checks are actually available to you right now, with the skills you already have from earlier modules?
explanation: False. There's a real middle ground between full understanding and blind trust: running it, reading any error carefully, checking the output against what you expected, and reading through the code line by line even without grasping every technique used. None of that requires expert-level understanding — it just requires actually looking, rather than either fully understanding or fully trusting. Refusing to use anything you don't already fully understand would rule out almost everything a beginner learns from, which defeats the purpose of asking for help at all.

prompt: An AI tool confidently tells you to use a function called `array.total()` to add up a list of numbers. You run it and get: `TypeError: array.total is not a function`. What actually happened?

options.text: You made a typo copying the function name
The AI generated a plausible-sounding function name that doesn't actually exist in JavaScript — this happens, confidently, sometimes
array.total() is real but requires a special setup you're missing
JavaScript changed recently and removed this function

hints: The error message itself, read using Module 4's skills, tells you plainly: array.total is not a function. That's not a setup problem.
AI tools generate text that sounds plausible based on patterns — that's a different process than checking a real, current reference for whether something exists.
explanation: The AI generated a function name that sounds entirely plausible — reads like something JavaScript might well have — but doesn't actually exist. This is a real, known failure mode sometimes called hallucination: generating confident, fluent-sounding text that isn't actually true, with no internal flag distinguishing it from a correct answer. The error message itself, read carefully using Module 4's skills, says so directly: `array.total is not a function`. Confidence in the original answer said nothing reliable about whether it was correct.

prompt: Sort each situation by whether it's a reasonable signal to double-check an AI's answer before trusting it.

categories: Not a strong signal either way

items.text: It confidently names a specific function or method you've never encountered before
It contradicts an error message you already read carefully
Two different AI answers to the same question disagree with each other
It's phrased politely and uses complete sentences
items.category: Not a strong signal either way

hints: Ask which of these tells you something about correctness, versus something about tone or presentation only.
Disagreement between two independent answers is a strong, concrete signal — at least one of them is wrong.
explanation: An unfamiliar specific claim, a direct contradiction with an error message you've already carefully read, and disagreement between multiple answers are all concrete, checkable signals worth pausing on. Politeness and sentence structure say nothing about correctness — a wrong answer and a right one can both be phrased equally well, which is exactly why tone isn't a reliable signal either way.

prompt: Two learners both get working code from an AI for the same problem. One pastes it in and moves on immediately. The other reads it, then closes the AI's answer and retypes the solution from memory, checking their version against the original after. Which one is more likely to be able to solve a similar problem alone next week?

options.text: Both equally — they both ended up with the same working code today
The one who retyped it from memory — producing something from memory is a different, stronger kind of practice than pasting it
The one who pasted it in, since they moved faster and covered more problems
Neither — AI-assisted learning doesn't transfer to working alone regardless of method

hints: This is the same recognition-versus-recall distinction from Module 1's lesson on the gap between knowing and doing.
Which learner actually generated the solution themselves at some point, even after seeing it once?
explanation: The one who retyped it from memory. This is Module 1's recognition-versus-recall distinction again, applied to AI help specifically: reading a working answer and pasting it trains recognizing that it's correct, but producing it again from memory — even having just seen it — is a genuinely different, stronger kind of practice, much closer to what solving a similar problem alone next week will actually require.

prompt: Describe your own personal rule for using AI help without losing the learning — one sentence, specific enough that you could actually follow it next time you ask for coding help.
hints: A useful rule names a concrete action (retype it, explain it back in your own words, note one new thing learned), not a vague intention like "try to understand it."
Think about what you'd actually be willing to do every time, not just on your most motivated day.
explanation: There's no single correct rule, but a genuinely useful one names a specific, repeatable action: retyping the solution from memory before moving on, explaining it back in your own words without looking at the original, or writing one sentence about what was newly learned from it. What weakens an answer is vagueness — "try to understand it better" isn't something you can check whether you actually did. The whole point of writing this down now is having a concrete habit ready before the next time an AI hands you a working answer.

prompt: Weak request: "My loop is broken." Which improvement adds the most missing information?

options.text: "My loop is really broken, please help soon"
"Here's my loop's code and the error it produces, and here's what I expected it to print instead"
"Loops are confusing, can you explain loops in general?"
"My loop is broken :("

hints: Urgency and tone don't add information about the actual problem — only the code, the error, and the expected result do.
explanation: Including the actual code, the actual error, and the expected result gives the AI three concrete anchors to work from. Urgency, a sad-face emoji, or a request for a general explanation of loops don't add anything about this specific broken loop.

prompt: Weak request: "This function doesn't work right." What's the single most useful addition?

options.text: "This function doesn't work right, and I've tried everything"
The actual function's code, plus what it currently outputs versus what it should output
A promise to rate the answer highly if it's correct
A request to "just rewrite it from scratch"

hints: "Doesn't work right" could mean the wrong output, an error, a crash, or something else entirely — which one is it?
explanation: The actual code plus the current-versus-expected output — this is the same expected-vs-actual anchor from lesson 1, and it's the single fact that turns "doesn't work right" from ambiguous into specific.

prompt: True or false: "Explain why this happens, then fix it" is a stronger request than "fix this" even when both include the same code and error.

config.statement: "Explain why this happens, then fix it" gets you more than "fix this," even with identical code and error attached.
config.rubric: A full answer confirms true and connects it to requesting reasoning specifically, not just more detail about the bug.

hints: The code and error being identical means the difference has to come from what's explicitly asked for.
One of these two requests explicitly asks for reasoning. The other doesn't.
explanation: True. With the underlying bug report held identical, the only variable left is what's explicitly asked for — and only one of the two phrasings requests the reasoning behind the fix. "Fix this" reliably gets a fix. "Explain why, then fix it" reliably gets both.

prompt: An AI answer includes a function name you've never seen before, stated with total confidence. What's the most reasonable next step?

options.text: Trust it completely — confidence is a reliable signal of correctness
Run it and see if it actually works, since confidence alone doesn't confirm correctness
Reject it automatically, since unfamiliar names are always a red flag
Ask a different AI tool the exact same question and just trust whichever answer sounds more confident

hints: Confidence in phrasing and correctness of content are two unrelated things — treating them as connected is exactly the trap lesson 4 covers.
explanation: Run it and see. Unfamiliarity plus confidence is exactly the situation worth checking, not automatically trusting or automatically rejecting — running it and reading any resulting error is a fast, concrete way to find out, using nothing beyond skills already built in this course.

prompt: Sort each check by whether it requires fully understanding the AI's code first, or can be done without full understanding.

items.text: Running it and seeing if it produces an error
Comparing the actual output to what you expected
Explaining, from memory, exactly why every individual line works the way it does
Reading it once for anything that looks obviously unfamiliar or off

hints: Running code and reading its output require zero mastery of the technique used — they're mechanical checks.
Explaining every line's reasoning from memory is a much higher bar than the other three.
explanation: Running it, comparing output, and a first read for anything obviously unfamiliar are all genuinely possible at any stage of learning — they're mechanical checks, not deep comprehension. Explaining every line's reasoning from memory is a different, higher bar, and not required before a first, real, useful check.

prompt: Weak request: "Can you write me a program?" Rewrite it with enough specifics that the answer would actually match what you want.
hints: Name the actual goal, not just "a program" — what should it do, specifically?
Mention your current skill level and anything you've already tried, if relevant.
explanation: A strong rewrite names the specific goal ("a program that adds up a list of grocery prices and prints the total"), and ideally any relevant constraints (what you've learned so far, what you'd like it to use). "Can you write me a program" with no further detail is the AI-help equivalent of "take care of the plant while I'm out" from Module 1 — technically a request, but with no checkable target attached.

prompt: You just got a working AI answer for a bug you were stuck on. What's the single most useful next action for actually learning from it?

options.text: Paste it in and immediately move to the next task
Close the answer and retype the solution from memory, then compare
Save the answer in a notes app and never look at it again
Ask the AI to make it more advanced, just to see what happens

hints: This is the exact recall-building action from lesson 5.
explanation: Retyping it from memory and comparing — this is the recall-building step that turns "I saw this once" into "I can produce this myself," which is the actual skill a future problem, with nothing pasted in front of you, will test.
